correctness.rationale: For each group size \(n\ge2\), the volunteer-minus-defector payoff is \(B(1-x)^{n-1}-C\); averaging produces a strictly decreasing selection gradient in \(x\) and a unique globally attracting interior root whenever \(0<C<B\). On four distinct sizes, the difference between any two probability mass vectors matching the zeroth through second raw moments is proportional to Lagrange barycentric weights \(w_i\), with proportionality equal to their third raw-moment difference. The generating-function difference equals that scalar times the third divided difference of \(f_q(n)=q^{n-1}\). For \(0<q<1\), the third derivative \((\log q)^3q^{n-1}\) is strictly negative, so the payoff and equilibrium comparisons hold for all such \(q\) and every permitted cost ratio. Vandermonde rank proves uniqueness for at most three sizes. For five, the displayed strictly positive laws match raw moments of orders zero through three but differ by \(q(1-q)^4/20\) in their generating functions. The boundary values \(q=0,1\) are treated separately; cost ratios satisfy \(0<C/B<1\). The extracted standard-library Fraction checker completed 2330 exact-rational assertions on 210 distinct four-size supports and both fully rational examples. Finite checks corroborate; interpolation establishes the universal statement.

value.rationale: Random-group-size N-volunteer dilemmas are motivated by empirical variation of social group sizes and Peña's 2011 finding that variance matters relative to a constant group. When comparing two nondegenerate populations with IDENTICAL mean AND variance, those prior comparisons alone provide no ranking. The new sharp support-size classification says exactly when third-moment data determine the direction of equilibrium movement uniformly across all benefits and costs, and identifies a concrete five-class failure even if the third moment is measured. The result is an all-parameter structural equilibrium comparator and an informative limitation of low-moment ecological/social summaries, rather than arbitrary small-case numerics or a routine modification of an existing bound. Real-world behavioral inference and unrestricted-support claims are expressly excluded.
